sections.title: Introduction

summary.text: Introduces FORML4, an autoformalization dataset for Lean 4 derived from Mathlib 4 theorems that pairs statements with proofs in both natural and formal languages, and proposes Process-Driven Autoformalization (PDA), which uses step-level Lean 4 compiler feedback to train a Process-Supervised Verifier (PSV) and iteratively refine statement autoformalization.

sections.extract: Autoformalization is the automatic conversion of natural language mathematics into formal lan- guages (Wang et al., 2018; Szegedy, 2020). It reduces the high cost of formalization and bridges the gap between automated mathematical reasoning research and the vast body of natural language mathematical knowledge (Wu et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2023c). Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) showed promising

sections.title: Related Work

summary.text: Reviews prior work on LLM-based autoformalization and outcome- versus process-supervised verifiers (OSV vs. PSV), contrasting expensive human or Monte Carlo Tree Search process annotation with PDA's use of automatic step-level feedback from the Lean 4 compiler.

sections.extract: Autoformalization with LLMs Autoformalization is the task of automatically converting informal theorems and proofs into machine-verifiable formats (Wang et al., 2018; Szegedy, 2020). Early approaches employed neural machine translation methods to translate texts into the Mizar lan- guage (Wang et al., 2020). Recent advancements in LLMs have opened up new possibilities for autoformalization. Researchers have explored

sections.title: FormL4: Dataset Construction

summary.text: Motivates the FORML4 benchmark by noting that existing Lean 4 autoformalization datasets rely on unchecked zero-shot GPT-4 informalization of theorem statements alone and omit proofs as context for dataset quality and evaluation.

Existing datasets (Jiang et al., 2023a; Ying et al., 2024a) aims to create benchmarks by informalizing formal theorems from existing libraries. summary.text: Describes the three-step iterative refinement cycle between the autoformalizer, the Lean 4 compiler, and the verifier: filtering autoformalizer outputs with the verifier for fine-tuning, compiling outputs from the improved autoformalizer to collect step-level feedback, and re-fine-tuning the verifier on the resulting higher-quality process-labeled data.

sections.title: Conclusion

summary.text: Concludes by summarizing the FORML4 benchmark and the Process-Driven Autoformalization (PDA) pipeline, noting future plans to extend the benchmark and method to Isabelle, HOL Light, and Coq, followed by the paper's bibliography.

sections.title: Future Directions

summary.text: Summarizes three experimental takeaways—the synergy of RFT+VEA, the superiority of process-supervised fine-tuning (PSV/PSV+) over outcome supervision, and the promise of iterative compiler-verifier-autoformalizer refinement—and identifies future work on refining process supervision and reducing RFT's compilation time overhead.

sections.title: More Related Works

summary.text: Provides extended related work covering interactive theorem provers and Lean 4, formal mathematics datasets across Coq, Isabelle, and Lean, prompting and verification techniques for LLM mathematical reasoning, and learning from human, internal, or tool-based feedback.

sections.extract: Formal Mathematics Formal languages, such as Isabelle (Wenzel et al., 2008), Lean (de Moura et al., 2015), HOL Light (Harrison, 1996), and Coq (Barras et al., 1997), have become integral tools in modern mathematics verification systems. These interactive theorem provers (ITPs) function as programming languages, allowing users to input statements and proofs in a formal language for automatic correctness verification.

sections.title: Detailed Decomposition Strategy

summary.text: Explains the three-step decomposition strategy for informalization—translating the formal statement into a natural-language problem, explaining each formal proof step's lemmas or tactics, and writing a standalone natural-language proof free of Lean 4 identifiers—so that the extracted problem and proof do not leak Lean 4 terms into the autoformalization input.

sections.extract: Our decomposition strategy for informalization involves instructing the model to perform the follow- ing subtasks sequentially: 1. sections.extract: The emergence of LLMs has fostered advancements in autoformalization tasks, where natural language descriptions are converted into formal, programmable constructs. In this analysis, we examine how various LLMs, benchmarking them across three different tests: Random, Basic, and Real proposed by FORML4. As shown in Table 15, there is a distinguishing performance divide between closed-source and open-source LLMs.
